item.title: The cryosphere beyond a planetary safe operating space
item.dc:creator: Rashid Sumaila, Johan Rockström, Deliang Chen, Ingo Fetzer, Haipeng Feng, Gustaf Hugelius, … (+25)
item.description:
Science — matched: cryosphere, irreversible, Holocene, Earth system
The cryosphere plays a vital role in regulating planetary dynamics and habitability, yet it remains unclear whether its essential functions remain within a safe operating space (SOS) amid Anthropocene change. Here, we propose a cryosphere SOS and systematically evaluate its contributions to Earth system resilience using the planetary boundaries framework. Multiple lines of evidence indicate an accelerating and partly irreversible loss of cryospheric integrity, driven by amplifying feedbacks. Key cryospheric control variables either have left or are committed to departing from Holocene-like conditions. We conclude that the cryosphere has breached its SOS and is on a trajectory that locks in long-term risks for human societies and ecosystems. Safeguarding planetary resilience therefore requires explicit consideration of cryosphere change and its interactions across the Earth system.

item.title: High-Resolution Cyclostratigraphy Uncovers Variable Orbital Forcing in the Oligocene South China Sea
item.dc:creator: Yiyang Zhou, Enze Xu, Xijun Liu, Shangfeng Zhang, Yaning Wang
item.description:
Geosciences — matched: orbital forcing
The Oligocene provides an important interval for examining climatic and sedimentary variability following the Eocene–Oligocene transition, but the expression of orbital forcing in low-latitude marginal seas remains incompletely understood. We integrate natural gamma-ray (GR) logging and microfossil records from Well L9 in the Pearl River Mouth Basin, northern South China Sea, to establish a cyclostratigraphic framework spanning approximately 34.6–21.7 Ma. A floating chronology based on 405 kyr cycle counting was anchored using an independently constrained Oligocene–Miocene boundary horizon. Spectral analyses identify approximately 405 kyr, 100 kyr, and 40 kyr components, together with longer-period variability near 2.4 Myr and 1.2 Myr. Amplitude-modulation analysis reveals an approximately 1.2 Myr component in the 40 kyr envelope, supporting an obliquity-related interpretation. In contrast, the 100 kyr envelope contains approximately 1.6 Myr variability rather than a clear 2.4 Myr component, leaving the eccentricity-modulation origin of the latter unresolved. Palynological evidence indicates generally cool and humid conditions during the early–middle Oligocene, followed by late Oligocene warming. Comparison with published climate records suggests correspondence with six recognized cooling episodes, although chronological uncertainty limits precise event alignment. These results provide a regional chronological and paleoenvironmental framework and highlight the need to distinguish observed long-period sedimentary variability from its proposed orbital origin.

item.title: Divergent Evolution Patterns of Glacier Meltwater and Implications for Downstream Water Utilization in Inland River Basins of the Northern Tibetan Plateau During 1976–2024
item.dc:creator: Mengyi Ji, Yuyan Zhou, Fan Lü, Yong Zhao, Lizhen Wang, Xinchun Ding, … (+2)
item.description:
Sustainability — matched: glacier, meltwater
The controls on glacier meltwater change and their implications for water supply risks remain unclear in glacier-fed inland river basins. We reconstructed glacier meltwater changes during 1976–2024 in eight representative basins of the northern Tibetan Plateau using a degree-day factor model and assessed its contribution to mountain-outlet runoff and downstream water use. Independent evaluation using the 2018 glacier inventory showed relative errors of 0.34–9.85% across the eight basins. Glacier storage decreased in all basins after the basin-specific segmentation years, while meltwater increased in most basins but declined in the Yarkand River Basin. These contrasting responses highlight substantial spatial differences in glacier meltwater evolution despite widespread glacier storage loss and increasing summer temperatures. The multi-year mean contribution of glacier meltwater to mountain-outlet runoff ranged from 1.2% to 54.3% across the eight basins, with declining contributions after the segmentation years in several highly glacierized basins. In the Hexi Corridor, annual glacier meltwater in the Shule River Basin was equivalent to about 20–40% of downstream water use. Glacier meltwater contributions to low-flow runoff increased in the three Hexi Corridor basins and in the Golmud and Buha River basins, but decreased in the Yarkand and Hotan River basins. These findings suggest potential implications of glacier storage loss for low-flow support and seasonal water supply risks, particularly in basins with substantial downstream irrigation and ecological water demands.

item.title: Tracking danger on the peaks
item.dc:creator: Miriam Jackson, Amrit Thapa
item.description:
Science — matched: cryosphere, permafrost
The Earth is warming, but not all regions are warming equally. In high mountain areas, temperatures are generally increasing by 1.5 to 2 times the global average, sometimes with devastating consequences. A small or gradual change in the mountain cryosphere—perhaps progressive thawing of frozen ground or a flood from a small glacial lake—can suddenly turn into a cascade of catastrophes with enormous ramifications. Monitoring systems for the cryosphere in high mountain areas have traditionally been designed to look at individual components and changes. What are the temperature and depth of the permafrost, or how much area is covered by snow, and what is the related avalanche danger? Many of the monitoring and warning systems were designed for historical patterns of snowfall or rainfall, and a river gauge may no longer be adequate if there is greater flow in the rainy season, or increased sediment that could damage the gauge.

item.title: Reef resilience and demise on the NW shelf of Australia during the warm Miocene
item.dc:creator: Benjamin Petrick, Lars Reuning, Or Mordechay Bialik, Lorenz Schwark, Miriam Pfeiffer
item.description:
Scientific Reports — matched: sea surface temperature, sediment core
Abstract During the Miocene, sea surface temperature (SSTs) and CO 2 exceeded modern levels. Given the current decline of coral reefs due to rising summer temperatures, it is unclear how extensive reef systems developed and thrived in a warm Miocene world. This problem is exacerbated by a lack of SST reconstructions. Here, we use TEX 86 H to reconstruct summer SSTs between 5.0 and 17.4 Ma from a sediment core (IODP Site U1464) within the Miocene NW Australian shelf Barrier Reef system. During the Miocene Climate Optimum, summer SSTs reached up to 34 °C. However, stable arid conditions and low subsidence rates allowed the reef to expand. Around 6 Ma, SSTs were ideal for coral reef growth, but increased terrestrial input and subsidence caused the relatively rapid collapse of almost all reefs. Multiple environmental stressors culminated in reef drowning. Therefore, a barrier reef system formed at > 30 °C SSTs, but this was only possible under otherwise ideal conditions.

item.title: A simple weather generator that converts statistical information from downscaled global climate models to sequences of daily precipitation and temperature
item.dc:creator: Rasmus E. Benestad
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
The paper presents two weather generators, one that generates sequences of daily precipitation based on two key statistical parameters and another that generates sequences of daily temperature based on the mean and standard deviation. They enable the use of downscaled projections of precipitation and temperature statistics for impact studies, such as hydrological modelling.
